findings.source_passage: each of the three setting up for a new legislator, a modern Lycurgus, or a brand-new Solon
findings.why_it_matters: The Lycurgus/Solon comparison is a characteristic piece of Cervantine ironic deflation—mocking the would-be lawmakers with classical allusion—and its erasure flattens the satirical register of the scene.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'each setting up for a new legislator, a modern Lycurgus, or a brand-new Solon' within the furnace-of-the-state passage.

findings.source_passage: no one now takes a nap, as they call it, without drawing his feet out of the stirrups, and leaning upon his lance, as the knights-errant used to do
findings.source_locator: Don Quixote's long speech on the degenerate knights, middle of the passage
findings.why_it_matters: The specific image of sleeping upright in the saddle, leaning on the lance, is an iconic chivalric motif that Don Quixote's speech deploys for satirical/elegiac effect; the draft skips from 'no one sleeps in the open field' to 'issuing from the wood,' losing this concrete and rhetorically distinctive detail.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the stirrups-and-lance nap image between the 'no one sleeps in full panoply' and 'issuing from the wood' clauses.

findings.source_passage: the light and glory of chivalry. These, or such as these, I would have to carry out my plan
findings.source_locator: End of Don Quixote's long enumeration of knights, before the Turk conclusion
findings.why_it_matters: The capping phrase 'the light and glory of chivalry' is a rhetorically climactic tag that closes Don Quixote's celebrated rhetorical list; the draft moves straight from the Ruggiero/Ferrara sentence to the plan, losing the peroration.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert 'were knights-errant, the light and glory of chivalry' as the closing flourish of the enumeration before 'These, or such as these, would carry out my plan.'

findings.source_passage: He was a graduate of Osuna in canon law; but even if he had been of Salamanca, it was the opinion of most people that he would have been mad all the same.
findings.source_locator: Opening of the barber's madhouse story
findings.why_it_matters: This is a famous satirical aside at the expense of the University of Osuna's reputation; its wit is the first joke of the embedded tale and is part of Cervantes' ironic texture. The draft omits it entirely, beginning only with the licentiate's confinement.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Osuna/Salamanca joke as the opening identification of the licentiate; it is too distinctive to cut.

findings.source_passage: I suspect it to be all fiction, fable, and falsehood, and dreams told by men awakened from sleep, or rather still half asleep.
findings.source_locator: Curate's expression of doubt about the reality of knights-errant
findings.why_it_matters: The curate's formulation 'fiction, fable, and falsehood, and dreams told by men awakened from sleep, or rather still half asleep' is interpretively important (it rehearses the novel's own self-questioning about fiction) and is rhetorically distinctive; the draft reduces it to the bare claim without the memorable phrasing.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the curate's exact formulation including the sleeping/half-asleep paradox when voicing his doubt about the reality of knights-errant.

findings.source_passage: supporting it upon the shoulders of the truth; which truth is so clear that I can almost say I have with my own eyes seen Amadis of Gaul
findings.source_locator: Don Quixote's reply on having seen Amadis
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'supporting it upon the shoulders of the truth' and the rhetorical build-up are lost; the draft jumps straight to the Amadis description, flattening the epistemological bravado that is characteristic of Don Quixote's voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain the 'shoulders of the truth' clause as a bridge before the Amadis portrait.

findings.source_passage: it is naturally the way with poets who have been scorned and rejected by their ladies, whether fictitious or not, in short by those whom they select as the ladies of their thoughts, to avenge themselves in satires and libels—a vengeance, to be sure, unworthy of generous hearts
findings.source_locator: Don Quixote's answer on satirists of Angelica
findings.why_it_matters: This generalizing observation on poets and vengeance is characteristic Cervantine ironic commentary on literary culture; the draft reduces his answer to bare summary, losing the digressive moral voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the aside on poets' retaliatory satires as 'unworthy of generous hearts' before the final sentence about Angelica.

summary: The draft preserves the narrative sequence and several verbatim passages well, but accumulates five medium-severity voice-flattening failures—including the loss of the Osuna/Salamanca joke, the curate's 'fiction, fable, and falsehood … dreams told by men half asleep' formulation, the Lycurgus/Solon satirical tag, the stirrups-and-lance nap image, and the 'light and glory of chivalry' peroration—which together constitute sufficient grounds for regeneration.
